problems.title: Gases on Titan
problems.statement:
Gas particles in a planetary atmosphere have a wide distribution of speeds. If the r.m.s. (root mean square) thermal speed of particles of a particular gas exceeds $1/6$ of the escape speed, then most of that gas will escape from the planet. What is the minimum atomic weight (relative atomic mass), $A_{\min}$, of an ideal monatomic gas so that it remains in the atmosphere of Titan?

Given, mass of Titan $M_{\mathrm{T}} = 1.23 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{kg}$, radius of Titan $R_{\mathrm{T}} = 2575\ \mathrm{km}$, surface temperature of Titan $T_{\mathrm{T}} = 93.7\ \mathrm{K}$.

solution.statement:
As the gas is monatomic,

$$\frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{T}} \approx \frac{1}{2}m_{\mathrm{g}}v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$$

$$3k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{T}} \approx \frac{M_{\mathrm{g}}}{N_{\mathrm{A}}}v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$$

$$\therefore\ v_{\mathrm{rms}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm{B}}N_{\mathrm{A}}T_{\mathrm{T}}}{M_{\mathrm{g}}}}$$

**[4.0]**

**50% deduction if 3/2 pre-factor is not used and 1/2 or 1 are used instead. Full credit if students writes the relation for $v_{\mathrm{rms}}$ directly.**

To remain in atmosphere,

$$v_{\mathrm{rms}} < \frac{v_{\mathrm{esc}}}{6} = \frac{1}{6}\sqrt{\frac{2GM_{\mathrm{T}}}{R_{\mathrm{T}}}}$$

$$\sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm{B}}N_{\mathrm{A}}T_{\mathrm{T}}}{M_{\mathrm{g}}}} < \sqrt{\frac{GM_{\mathrm{T}}}{18R_{\mathrm{T}}}}$$

$$\therefore\ M_{\mathrm{g}} > \frac{54k_{\mathrm{B}}N_{\mathrm{A}}T_{\mathrm{T}}R_{\mathrm{T}}}{GM_{\mathrm{T}}}$$ **[4.0]**

$$> \frac{54 \times 1.381 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 93.7 \times 2.575 \times 10^{6}}{6.6741 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.23 \times 10^{23}}\ \mathrm{g}$$

$$> 13.2\ \mathrm{g}$$ **[1.5]**

Thus, all gases with atomic weight more than $A_{\min} = 13.2$ will be retained in the atmosphere of Titan. **[0.5]**

**Half mark for understanding that atomic mass has no units.**

Alternative solution

$$\frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{T}} \approx \frac{1}{2}m_{\mathrm{g}}v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$$

$$\therefore\ v_{\mathrm{rms}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{T}}}{m_{\mathrm{g}}}}$$ **[4.0]**

$$\therefore\ m_{\mathrm{g}} > \frac{54k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{T}}R_{\mathrm{T}}}{GM_{\mathrm{T}}}$$ **[4.0]**

$$m_{\mathrm{g}} > 2.19 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\therefore\ A_{\min} = \frac{m_{\mathrm{g}}}{\mathrm{atomic\ mass\ unit}} = \frac{2.19 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}}$$

$$A_{\min} = 13.2$$ **[1.0]**

**Answers between 13.0 and 13.4 are acceptable with full credit.**

problems.title: Early Universe
problems.statement: Cosmological models indicate that radiation energy density, $\rho_{\mathrm{r}}$, in the Universe is proportional to $(1+\mathrm{z})^{4}$, and the matter energy density, $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, is proportional to $(1+\mathrm{z})^{3}$, where $\mathrm{z}$ is the redshift. The dimensionless density parameter, $\Omega$, is given as $\Omega = \rho/\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$, where $\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the critical energy density of the Universe. In the present Universe, the density parameters corresponding to radiation and matter, are $\Omega_{\mathrm{r_0}} = 10^{-4}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m_0}} = 0.3$, respectively.

parts.label: T3.1
parts.statement: Calculate the redshift, $\mathrm{z_e}$, at which radiation and matter energy densities were equal.

parts.label: T3.2
parts.statement: Assuming that the radiation from the early Universe has a blackbody spectrum with a temperature of 2.732 K, estimate the temperature, $T_{\mathrm{e}}$, of the radiation at redshift $\mathrm{z_e}$.

parts.label: T3.3
parts.statement: Estimate the typical photon energy, $E_{\nu}$ (in eV), of the radiation as emitted at redshift $\mathrm{z_e}$.

solution.statement:
**T3.1:**

$$\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{mo}}/\rho_{\mathrm{c}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{ro}}/\rho_{\mathrm{c}}} = \frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}_0}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{r}_0}} = \frac{0.3}{10^{-4}} = 3000$$

At $z_{\mathrm{e}}$, both matter density and radiation density were equal.

$$\rho_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho_{\mathrm{m}}$$

$$\therefore\ \rho_{\mathrm{r}_0}(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^4 = \rho_{\mathrm{m}_0}(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^3$$

$$1+z_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{m}_0}}{\rho_{\mathrm{r}_0}} = 3000$$ **[2.0]**

$$\therefore\ z_{\mathrm{e}} \simeq 3000$$ **[1.0]**

**Only $z_{\mathrm{e}} = 2999$ and $z_{\mathrm{e}} = 3000$ are acceptable answers.**

**T3.2:**

As the Universe behaves like an ideal black body, the radiation density will be proportional to the fourth power of the temperature (Stefan's law).

$$\left(\frac{T_{\mathrm{e}}}{T_0}\right)^4 = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{re}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{r}_0}}$$

$$= \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{r}_0}(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^4}{\rho_{\mathrm{r}_0}}$$ **[2.0]**

$$\left(\frac{T_{\mathrm{e}}}{2.732}\right)^4 = (1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^4$$ **[1.0]**

$$\frac{T_{\mathrm{e}}}{2.732} = 1+z_{\mathrm{e}} = 3000$$

$$T_{\mathrm{e}} = 3000 \times 2.732$$

$$T_{\mathrm{e}} = 8200\ \mathrm{K}$$ **[1.0]**

**$8100 \leq T_{\mathrm{e}} \leq 8200$ gives 1.0; $8200 < T_{\mathrm{e}} \leq 9000$ gives 0.5; else 0.**

**T3.3:**

Wien's law:

$$\lambda_{\max} = \frac{0.002898\ \mathrm{m\ K}}{T_e}$$

$$= \frac{0.002898}{\frac{8200}{}}\ \mathrm{m} = 354\ \mathrm{nm}$$ **[1.0]**

$$E_{\nu} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\max}}$$

$$= \frac{6.62 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{354 \times 10^{-9}}\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{5.62 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **[1.0]**

$$E_{\nu} = 3.5\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **[1.0]**

Alternative solution:

$$E_{\nu} = k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{e}}$$

$$= 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 8200\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{1.13 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **[2.0]**

$$E_{\nu} = 0.71\ \mathrm{eV}$$ **[1.0]**

**Use of either Wien's law or $E = k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ gets full credit. $E_{\nu} = 3k_{\mathrm{B}}T/2$ or similar gets no credit. Answers with $E_{\nu} = 3k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ or $E_{\nu} = 2.7k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ also get full credit.**

problems.title: Shadows
problems.statement:
An observer in the northern hemisphere noticed that the length of the shortest shadow of a 1.000 m vertical stick on a day was 1.732 m. On the same day, the length of the longest shadow of the same vertical stick was measured to be 5.671 m.

Find the latitude, $\phi$, of the observer and declination of the Sun, $\delta_{\odot}$, on that day. Assume the Sun to be a point source and ignore atmospheric refraction.

solution.statement:
As the longest shadow of the Sun on the given day is of finite length, the Sun is circumpolar for this observer on this day. **[2.0]**

In the figure above, the left panel shows the shadow $OS$ formed by stick $OA$ (of length 1.000 m), and the right panel shows the Sun's location in two cases.

For an altitude $\theta$ of the Sun,

$$\tan\theta = \frac{OA}{OS} = \frac{1.000\ \mathrm{m}}{OS}$$

$$\therefore\ \cot\theta = OS\ (\mathrm{in\ metres})$$ **[1.0]**

Let $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be altitude in two extreme cases.

$$\theta_1 = 180^{\circ} - \phi - (90^{\circ} - \delta_{\odot}) = 90^{\circ} - \phi + \delta_{\odot}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\cot(90^{\circ} - \phi + \delta_{\odot}) = 1.732$$

$$\therefore\ \tan(\phi - \delta_{\odot}) = 1.732$$

$$\phi - \delta_{\odot} = \tan^{-1}(1.732) = 60^{\circ} = 1.047\ \mathrm{rad}$$ **[1.5]**

$$\theta_2 = \phi - (90^{\circ} - \delta_{\odot}) = \phi - 90^{\circ} + \delta_{\odot}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\cot(\phi - 90^{\circ} + \delta_{\odot}) = 5.671$$

$$\therefore\ \tan(\phi - 90^{\circ} + \delta_{\odot}) = \frac{1}{5.671}$$

$$\phi + \delta_{\odot} = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5.671}\right) + 90^{\circ} = 100^{\circ} = 1.745\ \mathrm{rad}$$ **[1.5]**

Solving,

$$\phi = 80^{\circ} = 1.396\ \mathrm{rad}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\delta_{\odot} = 20^{\circ} = 0.349\ \mathrm{rad}$$ **[1.0]**

**Given high accuracy of shadow length, only ±0.5° is allowed.**

One can also solve the question by manipulating $\tan(\phi - \delta_{\odot})$ and $\tan(\phi + \delta_{\odot})$, to get $\tan(\phi)$ and $\tan(\delta_{\odot})$.

figures.caption: In the figure above, the left panel shows the shadow OS formed by stick OA (of length 1.000 m), and the right panel shows the Sun's location in two cases.
figures.alt: Left panel: vertical stick OA with shadow OS and altitude angle θ. Right panel: celestial dome showing latitude φ, the Sun's circumpolar path with arcs labelled 90 − δ_☉ and two shadow/altitude angles θ₁ and θ₂.

problems.title: GMRT beam transit
problems.statement:
Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT), one of the world's largest radio telescopes at metre wavelengths, is located in western India (latitude: 19°6' N, longitude: 74°3' E). GMRT consists of 30 dish antennas, each with a diameter of 45.0 m. A single dish of GMRT was held fixed with its axis pointing at a zenith angle of 39°42' along the northern meridian such that a radio point source would pass along a diameter of the beam, when it is transiting the meridian.

What is the duration $T_{\mathrm{transit}}$ for which this source would be within the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the beam of a single GMRT dish observing at 200 MHz?

**Hint:** The FWHM size of the beam of a radio dish operating at a given frequency corresponds to the angular resolution of the dish. Assume uniform illumination.

solution.statement:
As the dish is pointed towards northern meridian at zenith angle of $39.7^{\circ}$, altitude of the centre of the beam is

$$a = 90.00^{\circ} - z = 90.00^{\circ} - 39.70^{\circ} = 50.30^{\circ}$$ **[1.0]**

Thus, declination of the source should be,

$$\delta = 90.00 - a + \phi = 90.00^{\circ} - 50.30^{\circ} + 19.10^{\circ} = 58.80^{\circ}$$ **[2.0]**

**Declination = ZA + Latitude also gets full credit.**

FWHM beam size (for uniform illumination) will be given by

$$\theta = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}$$ **[1.5]**

$$= \frac{1.22c}{D\nu} = \frac{1.22 \times 2.998 \times 10^8}{45.0 \times 2 \times 10^8}$$

$$= 0.0406\ \mathrm{rad}$$

$$\theta = 2.33^{\circ}$$ **[1.5]**

$$T_{\mathrm{transit}} = \frac{\theta \times 3.99\ \mathrm{min}}{\cos\delta}$$ **[3.0]**

$$= \frac{2.33 \times 3.99\ \mathrm{min}}{\cos 58.8}$$

$$T_{\mathrm{transit}} = 17.9\ \mathrm{min}$$ **[1.0]**

- **Use of 4 min per degree is also acceptable.**
- **Missing $\cos\delta$ gets a penalty of 2.0.**

problems.title: Cepheid Pulsations
problems.statement: The star $\beta$-Doradus is a Cepheid variable star with a pulsation period of 9.84 days. We make a simplifying assumption that the star is brightest when it is most contracted (radius being $R_1$) and it is faintest when it is most expanded (radius being $R_2$). For simplicity, assume that the star maintains its spherical shape and behaves as a perfect black body at every instant during the entire cycle. The bolometric magnitude of the star varies from 3.46 to 4.08. From Doppler measurements, we know that during pulsation the stellar surface expands or contracts at an average radial speed of 12.8 km s$^{-1}$. Over the period of pulsation, the peak of thermal radiation (intrinsic) of the star varies from 531.0 nm to 649.1 nm.

parts.label: T6.1
parts.statement: Find the ratio of radii of the star in its most contracted and most expanded states ($R_1/R_2$).

parts.label: T6.2
parts.statement: Find the radii of the star (in metres) in its most contracted and most expanded states ($R_1$ and $R_2$).

parts.label: T6.3
parts.statement: Calculate the flux of the star, $F_2$, when it is in its most expanded state.

parts.label: T6.4
parts.statement: Find the distance to the star, $D_{\mathrm{star}}$, in parsecs.

solution.statement:
**(T6.1)** Find the ratio of radii of the star in its most contracted and most expanded states $(R_1/R_2)$. **[7]**

**Solution:**
We first find flux ratio and then use Stefan's law to compare the fluxes.

$$m_1 - m_2 = -2.5\log\left(\frac{F_1}{F_2}\right) \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{F_1}{F_2} = 10^{-0.4(m_1-m_2)} = 10^{-0.4(3.46-4.08)}$$

$$= 1.77 \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$L_i = 4\pi R_i^2 \sigma T_i^4 \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$\therefore\ F_1 = \frac{4\pi R_1^2 \sigma T_1^4}{4\pi D^2} \qquad F_2 = \frac{4\pi R_2^2 \sigma T_2^4}{4\pi D^2} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{R_1^2}{R_2^2} \times \frac{T_1^4}{T_2^4}$$

$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \sqrt{\frac{F_1}{F_2}} \times \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$$

From Wien's displacement law, $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$. **[1.0]**

$$\therefore\ \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \sqrt{\frac{F_1}{F_2}} \times \left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\right)^2 \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$= \sqrt{1.77} \times \left(\frac{531.0}{649.1}\right)^2$$

$$\boxed{\frac{R_1}{R_2} = 0.890} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

**Acceptable range:** $\pm 0.010$.

**(T6.2)** Find the radii of the star (in metres) in its most contracted and most expanded states $(R_1$ and $R_2)$. **[3]**

**Solution:**

$$R_2 - R_1 = v \times P/2 \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

$$R_2 - R_1 = 12.8 \times 10^3 \times 86\,400 \times \frac{9.84}{2}\ \mathrm{m}$$

$$(1 - 0.890)R_2 = 5.441 \times 10^9\ \mathrm{m}$$

$$\therefore\ \boxed{R_2 = 4.95 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}} \quad \textbf{[0.5]}$$

$$\boxed{R_1 = 4.41 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}} \quad \textbf{[0.5]}$$

**Acceptable range:** $\pm 0.02 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for both.

**(T6.3)** Calculate the flux of the star, $F_2$, when it is in its most expanded state. **[5]**

**Solution:**
To get the absolute value of flux $(F_2)$ we must compare it with observed flux of the Sun.

$$m_2 - m_\odot = -2.5\log\left(\frac{F_2}{F_\odot}\right)$$

$$\therefore\ F_2 = F_\odot\, 10^{-0.4(m_2-m_\odot)} \quad \textbf{[3.0]}$$

$$= \frac{L_\odot}{4\pi a_\oplus^2} \times 10^{-0.4(4.08+26.72)}$$

$$= \frac{3.826 \times 10^{26} \times 4.7863 \times 10^{-13}}{4\pi (1.496 \times 10^{11})^2}\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-2}}$$

$$\boxed{F_2 = 6.51 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-2}}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

**Acceptable range:** $\pm 0.04 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-2}}$.

**(T6.4)** Find the distance to the star, $D_{\mathrm{star}}$, in parsecs. **[5]**

**Solution:**

$$D_{\mathrm{star}} = \sqrt{\frac{L_2}{4\pi F_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{R_2^2 \sigma T_2^4}{F_2}} = R_2 T_2^2 \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{F_2}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

Wien's law: $T_2 = \dfrac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}}{\lambda_2}$ **[1.0]**

$$D_{\mathrm{star}} = 4.95 \times 10^{10} \times \left(\frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{649.1 \times 10^{-9}}\right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{5.670 \times 10^{-8}}{6.51 \times 10^{-10}}}$$

$$\therefore\ \boxed{D_{\mathrm{star}} = 9.208 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{m} = 298\ \mathrm{pc}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

**Acceptable range:** $298 \pm 2\ \mathrm{pc}$ (depends on truncation).

problems.title: Telescope optics
problems.statement:
In a particular ideal refracting telescope of focal ratio $f$/5, the focal length of the objective lens is 100 cm and that of the eyepiece is 1 cm.

An introduction of a concave lens (Barlow lens) between the objective lens and the prime focus is a common way to increase the magnification without a large increase in the length of the telescope. A Barlow lens of focal length 1 cm is now introduced between the objective and the eyepiece to double the magnification.

A telescope is now constructed with the same objective lens and a CCD detector placed at the prime focus (without any Barlow lens or eyepiece). The size of each pixel of the CCD detector is 10 μm.

parts.label: T7.1
parts.statement: What is the angular magnification, $m_0$, of the telescope? What is the length of the telescope, $L_0$, i.e. the distance between its objective and eyepiece?

parts.label: T7.2
parts.statement: At what distance, $d_{\mathrm{B}}$, from the prime focus must the Barlow lens be kept in order to obtain this desired double magnification?

parts.label: T7.3
parts.statement: What is the increase, $\Delta L$, in the length of the telescope?

parts.label: T7.4
parts.statement: What will be the distance in pixels between the centroids of the images of the two stars , $n_{\mathrm{p}}$, on the CCD, if they are 20'' apart on the sky?

solution.statement:
**(T7.1)** What is the angular magnification, $m_0$, of the telescope? What is the length of the telescope, $L_0$, i.e. the distance between its objective and eyepiece? **[4]**

**Solution:**
The magnification will be given by,

$$m_0 = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$= \frac{100}{1} = 100 \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

The magnification is $\boxed{m_0 = 100}$

Length of the telescope will be

$$L_0 = f_o + f_e \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$= 100 + 1 = 101\ \mathrm{cm} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

The telescope length will be $\boxed{L_0 = 101\ \mathrm{cm}}$

**Exact answer required for credit.**

**(T7.2)** At what distance, $d_{\mathrm{B}}$, from the prime focus must the Barlow lens be kept in order to obtain this desired double magnification? **[6]**

**Solution:**
We use the following sign convention. Lens is the origin. Direction along the direction of light is taken as positive. The lens formula is $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u}$ ($f$ is positive for convex lens and negative for concave lens). Magnification is $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$. Solutions using other sign conventions are acceptable.

Let $v$ be image distance from the Barlow lens.

$$\frac{1}{f_{\mathrm{B}}} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

Distance of Barlow lens, $d_{\mathrm{B}}$, before the prime focus is same as the object distance, $u$, in this case. **[1.0]**

$$\frac{1}{f_{\mathrm{B}}} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{d_B}$$

Also, $m_{\mathrm{B}} = 2 = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{v}{d_{\mathrm{B}}}$ **[0.5]**

$$\therefore\ \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{B}}} = \frac{2}{v} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{1}{-1} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{2}{v}$$

$$-1 = \frac{-1}{v}$$

$$v = 1\ \mathrm{cm}$$

$$d_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{v}{2} = \frac{1\ \mathrm{cm}}{2} = 0.5\ \mathrm{cm} \quad \textbf{[2.5]}$$

The positive sign for $d_{\mathrm{B}}$ indicates that the Barlow lens was introduced $\boxed{0.5\ \mathrm{cm}}$ before the prime focus.

**(T7.3)** What is the increase, $\Delta L$, in the length of the telescope? **[4]**

**Solution:**
The increase in the length will be,

$$\Delta L = v - d_{\mathrm{B}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

$$= 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5\ \mathrm{cm} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

Thus, the length will be increased by $\boxed{\Delta L = 0.5\ \mathrm{cm}}$

**(T7.4)** What will be the distance in pixels between the centroids of the images of the two stars, $n_{\mathrm{p}}$, on the CCD, if they are $20''$ apart on the sky? **[6]**

**Solution:**
Plate scale at prime focus is given by,

$$s = \frac{1}{f_o} = \frac{1\ \mathrm{rad}}{1\ \mathrm{m}} = 0.206\,265\ \mathrm{arcsec/\mu m} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

Since each pixel is $10\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ in size,

$$s_{\mathrm{p}} = 10 \times 0.206\ \mathrm{arcsec/\mu m} = 2.06\ \mathrm{arcsec/pixel} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

Two stars will be separated by,

$$n_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{20''}{2.06''}\ \mathrm{pixels} \simeq \boxed{10\ \mathrm{pixels}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

**Acceptable range: 9.5 to 10.5 pixels.**

problems.title: U-Band photometry
problems.statement:
A star has an apparent magnitude $m_{\mathrm{U}} = 15.0$ in the $U$-band. The $U$-band filter is ideal, i.e., it has perfect (100%) transmission within the band and is completely opaque (0% transmission) outside the band. The filter is centered at 360 nm, and has a width of 80 nm. It is assumed that the star also has a flat energy spectrum with respect to frequency. The conversion between magnitude, $m$, in any band and flux density, $f$, of a star in Jansky ($1\ \mathrm{Jy} = 1 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{W\ Hz^{-1}\ m^{-2}}$) is given by

$$f = 3631 \times 10^{-0.4m}\ \mathrm{Jy}$$

This star is being observed in the $U$-band using a ground based telescope, whose primary mirror has a diameter of 2.0 m. Atmospheric extinction in $U$-band during the observation is 50%. You may assume that the seeing is diffraction limited. Average surface brightness of night sky in $U$-band was measured to be 22.0 mag/arcsec$^2$.

parts.label: T8.1
parts.statement: Approximately how many $U$-band photons, $N_0$, from this star will be incident normally on a 1 m$^2$ area at the top of the Earth's atmosphere every second?

parts.label: T8.2
parts.statement: What is the ratio, $R$, of number of photons received per second from the star to that received from the sky, when measured over a circular aperture of diameter 2''?

parts.label: T8.3
parts.statement: In practice, only 20% of U-band photons falling on the primary mirror are detected. How many photons, $N_{\mathrm{t}}$, from the star are detected per second?

solution.statement:
**(T8.1)** Approximately how many $U$-band photons, $N_0$, from this star will be incident normally on a $1\ \mathrm{m^2}$ area at the top of the Earth's atmosphere every second? **[8]**

**Solution:**
The $U$-band is defined as $(360 \pm 40)\ \mathrm{nm}$. Thus, the maximum, minimum and average frequencies of the band will be,

$$\nu_{\max} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{\max}} = 9.369 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$$

$$\nu_{\min} = 7.495 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$$

$$\nu_{\mathrm{avg}} = 8.432 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$$

$$\Delta\nu = \nu_{\max} - \nu_{\min}$$

$$= 1.874 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

$$f_{\mathrm{st1}} = 3631 \times 10^{-0.4 \times 15} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

$$= 3.631\ \mathrm{mJy} = 3.631 \times 10^{-29}\ \mathrm{W\ Hz^{-1}\ m^{-2}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

Now, $N_0 \times h\nu_{\mathrm{avg}} = \Delta\nu \times f_{\mathrm{st1}} \times A \times \Delta t$ **[2.0]**

where, $A = 1\ \mathrm{m^2}$ & $\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{s}$

$$\therefore\ N_0 = \frac{1.874 \times 10^{14} \times 3.631 \times 10^{-29}}{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 8.432 \times 10^{14}}$$

$$\simeq \boxed{12180} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

**Exact calculation including integration is accepted with full credit (exact answer: 12190).**
**Accepted range:** $12180 \pm 200$.
**Using flat spectrum for $\Delta\lambda$ instead of $\Delta\nu$ is considered a major conceptual error, and will incur penalty of 2.0 marks.**

**(T8.2)** What is the ratio, $R$, of number of photons received per second from the star to that received from the sky, when measured over a circular aperture of diameter $2''$? **[8]**

**Solution:**
Let us call sky flux per square arcsec as $\Phi$ and total sky flux for the given aperture as $\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}$. Let total star flux be $\phi_{st}$.

$$\phi_{\mathrm{sky}} = A\Phi = \pi \times (1\ \mathrm{arcsec})^2 \times \Phi = \pi\Phi \quad \textbf{[3.0]}$$

$$\therefore\ m_{\mathrm{sky}} = 22.0 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\frac{\Phi}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}}\right) \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$= 22.0 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\frac{\Phi}{\pi\Phi}\right)$$

$$= 22.0 - 2.5\log_{10}(\pi)$$

$$m_{\mathrm{sky}} = 20.76\ \mathrm{mag} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

As extinction is 50% **[1.0]**

$$R = \frac{\phi_{\mathrm{st2}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}} = \frac{0.5\phi_{\mathrm{st1}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}} = 0.5 \times 10^{(20.76-15)/2.5}$$

$$\simeq \boxed{100} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

**Accepted range:** $\pm 5$.
**A student may also calculate number of photons incident per second per metre square in this case and then compare it with the answer in the first case to get the correct ratio.**

**(T8.3)** In practice, only 20% of $U$-band photons falling on the primary mirror are detected. How many photons, $N_{\mathrm{t}}$, from the star are detected per second? **[4]**

**Solution:**

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} \times 1\ \mathrm{m^2} = N_0 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times A_{\mathrm{t}} \quad \textbf{[2.0]}$$

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} = 12180 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times \pi\left(\frac{2.0}{2}\right)^2 = 1233\pi \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} \simeq \boxed{3813} \quad \textbf{[1.0]}$$

**Accepted range** $(3813 \pm 50)$.

**(T8.2)**

Solution:

Let us call sky flux per square arcsec as $\dot{\Phi}$ and total sky flux for the given aperture as $\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}$. Let total star flux be $\phi_{st}$.

$$\phi_{\mathrm{sky}} = A\dot{\Phi} = \pi \times (1\ \mathrm{arcsec})^2 \times \dot{\Phi} = \pi\dot{\Phi}$$ **[3.0]**

$$\therefore\ m_{\mathrm{sky}} = 22.0 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\frac{\dot{\Phi}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}}\right)$$ **[1.0]**

$$= 22.0 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\frac{\dot{\Phi}}{\pi\dot{\Phi}}\right) = 22.0 - 2.5\log_{10}\left(\pi\right)$$

$$m_{\mathrm{sky}} = 20.76\ \mathrm{mag}$$ **[1.0]**

As extinction is 50% **[1.0]**

$$R = \frac{\phi_{\mathrm{st2}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}} = \frac{0.5\phi_{\mathrm{st1}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}} = 0.5 \times 10^{(20.76-15)/2.5} \simeq \boxed{100}$$ **[2.0]**

**Accepted range:** ±5.

**A student may also calculate number of photons incident per second per metre square in this case and then compare it with the answer in the first case to get the correct ratio.**

**(T8.3)**

Solution:

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} \times 1\ \mathrm{m^2} = N_0 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times A_{\mathrm{t}}$$ **[2.0]**

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} = 12180 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times \pi\left(\frac{2.0}{2}\right)^2 = 1233\pi$$ **[1.0]**

$$N_{\mathrm{t}} \simeq \boxed{3813}$$ **[1.0]**

**Accepted range** (3813 ± 50).

**Use of approximation with proper justification at a later stage than at the first step will get full credit.**

If penalty has already been imposed in part (T12.6), no further penalty for lack of approximation.

problems.title: Mars Orbiter Mission
problems.statement:
India's Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) was launched using the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) on 5 November 2013. The dry mass of MOM (body + instruments) was 500 kg and it carried fuel of mass 852 kg. It was initially placed in an elliptical orbit around the Earth with perigee at a height of 264.1 km and apogee at a height of 23903.6 km, above the surface of the Earth. After raising the orbit six times, MOM was transferred to a trans-Mars injection orbit (Hohmann orbit).

The first such orbit-raising was performed by firing the engines for a very short time near the perigee. The engines were fired to change the orbit without changing the plane of the orbit and without changing its perigee. This gave a net impulse of $1.73 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{kg\ m\ s^{-1}}$ to the satellite. Ignore the change in mass due to burning of fuel.

parts.label: T9.1
parts.statement: What is the height of the new apogee, $h_{\mathrm{a}}$ above the surface of the Earth, after this engine burn?

parts.label: T9.2
parts.statement: Find the eccentricity ($e$) of the new orbit after the burn and the new orbital period ($P$) of MOM in hours.

solution.statement:
**(T9.1) What is the height of the new apogee, $h_{\mathrm{a}}$, above the surface of the Earth, after this engine burn?**

Solution:

Let apogee and perigee distances be $r_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ respectively.

$$r_{\mathrm{p}} = R_{\oplus} + h_{\mathrm{p}}^{i} = (6371 + 264)\ \mathrm{km} = 6635\ \mathrm{km}$$ **[1.0]**

$$r_{\mathrm{a}} = R_{\oplus} + h_{\mathrm{a}}^{i} = (6371 + 23904)\ \mathrm{km} = 30275\ \mathrm{km}$$ **[1.0]**

Conservation of energy and angular momentum gives

$$E = -\frac{GmM_{\oplus}}{r_{\mathrm{p}} + r_{\mathrm{a}}}$$

Total energy at perigee

$$\frac{1}{2}m{v_{\mathrm{p}}}^2 - \frac{GmM_{\oplus}}{r_{\mathrm{p}}} = E = -\frac{GmM_{\oplus}}{r_{\mathrm{p}} + r_{\mathrm{a}}}$$

$$\frac{1}{2}{v_{\mathrm{p}}}^2 = \frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r_{\mathrm{p}}}\left(1 - \frac{r_{\mathrm{p}}}{r_{\mathrm{p}} + r_{\mathrm{a}}}\right)$$

$$\therefore\ v_{\mathrm{p}} = \sqrt{2\frac{GM_{\oplus}\ r_{\mathrm{a}}}{r_{\mathrm{a}} + r_{\mathrm{p}}}\ r_{\mathrm{p}}}$$ **[2.0]**

$$= \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.972 \times 10^{24} \times 3.0275 \times 10^7}{6.635 \times 10^6 \times (3.0275 + 6.635 \times 10^6)}}$$

$$= 9.929\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$$ **[1.0]**

As the engine burn is just 41.6 s, we assume that the entire impulse is applied instantaneously at perigee. The impulse is $J = 1.73 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{kg\ m\ s^{-1}}$. Note that the total mass of MOM must include the fuel, so we have to use $m = 500 + 852 = 1352\ \mathrm{kg}$. **[1.0]**

Change in velocity due to impulse at perigee is

$$\Delta v = \frac{J}{m} = \frac{1.73 \times 10^5}{1352} = 128.0\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$$ **[1.0]**

The new velocity will be given by (we use $'$ symbol to denote quantities after the first orbit-raising maneuvre)

$$v_{\mathrm{p}}' = v_{\mathrm{p}} + \Delta v = 10.06\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$$ **[1.0]**

The perigee remains unchanged. So we get $r_{\mathrm{p}}' = r_{\mathrm{p}}$.

Since the satellite is moving faster, the new apogee will be higher.

$$v_{\mathrm{p}}' = \sqrt{2GM_{\oplus}\frac{r_{\mathrm{a}}'}{r_{\mathrm{p}}'(r_{\mathrm{a}}' + r_{\mathrm{p}}')}}$$

$$\therefore\ 1 + \frac{r_{\mathrm{p}}'}{r_{\mathrm{a}}'} = \frac{2GM_{\oplus}}{(v_{\mathrm{p}}')^2 \times r_{\mathrm{p}}'}$$ **[2.0]**

$$= \frac{2 \times 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.972 \times 10^{24}}{(10.06 \times 10^3)^2 \times 6.635 \times 10^6} = 1.188$$

$$r_{\mathrm{a}}' = \frac{6635}{0.188} = 35\,380\ \mathrm{km}$$ **[2.0]**

$$h_{\mathrm{a}} = 35380 - 6371 = \boxed{29\,009\ \mathrm{km}}$$ **[1.0]**

**Acceptable range:** ±150 km

**(T9.2) Find eccentricity ($e$) of the new orbit after the burn and new orbital period ($P$) of MOM in hours.**

Solution:

As seen above,

$$\frac{r_{\mathrm{p}}'}{r_{\mathrm{a}}'} = 0.188 = \frac{1 - e}{1 + e}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\therefore\ e = \frac{1 - 0.188}{1 + 0.188} = \boxed{0.683}$$ **[1.0]**

**Acceptable range:** ±0.002

The new orbital semi-major axis and orbital period will be,

$$a' = \frac{r_{\mathrm{a}}' + r_{\mathrm{p}}'}{2}$$ **[1.0]**

$$= \frac{35380 + 6635}{2} = 20\,933\ \mathrm{km}$$ **[1.0]**

$$P = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a'^3}{GM_{\oplus}}}$$ **[1.0]**

$$= 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(2.0933 \times 10^7)^3}{6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.972 \times 10^{24}}} = \boxed{30\,136\ \mathrm{s} = 8.37\ \mathrm{h}}$$ **[1.0]**

**Acceptable range:** ±0.1 h

problems.title: Gravitational Lensing Telescope
problems.statement:
Einstein's General Theory of Relativity predicts bending of light around massive bodies. For simplicity, we assume that the bending of light happens at a single point for each light ray, as shown in the figure. The angle of bending, $\theta_{\mathrm{b}}$, is given by

$$\theta_{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}}{r}$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sch}}$ is the Schwarzschild radius associated with that gravitational body. We call $r$, the distance of the incoming light ray from the parallel $x$-axis passing through the centre of the body, as the "impact parameter".

A massive body thus behaves somewhat like a focusing lens. The light rays coming from infinite distance beyond a massive body, and having the same impact parameter $r$, converge at a point along the axis, at a distance $f_r$ from the centre of the massive body. An observer at that point will benefit from huge amplification due to this gravitational focusing. The massive body in this case is being used as a Gravitational Lensing Telescope for amplification of distant signals.

figures.alt: Schematic of gravitational deflection: a parallel light ray is bent by angle θ_b at a point above the gravitating body (grey circle), with impact parameter r marked against the horizontal x-axis passing through the centre of the body.

parts.label: T10.1
parts.statement: Consider the possibility of our Sun as a gravitational lensing telescope. Calculate the shortest distance, $f_{\min}$, from the centre of the Sun (in A.U.) at which the light rays can get focused.

parts.label: T10.2
parts.statement:
Consider a small circular detector of radius $a$, kept at a distance $f_{\min}$ centered on the $x$-axis and perpendicular to it. Note that only the light rays which pass within a certain annulus (ring) of width $h$ (where $h \ll R_{\odot}$) around the Sun would encounter the detector. The amplification factor at the detector is defined as the ratio of the intensity of the light incident on the detector in the presence of the Sun and the intensity in the absence of the Sun.

Express the amplification factor, $A_{\mathrm{m}}$, at the detector in terms of $R_{\odot}$ and $a$.

parts.label: T10.3
parts.statement:
Consider a spherical mass distribution, such as dark matter in a galaxy cluster, through which light rays can pass while undergoing gravitational bending. Assume for simplicity that for the gravitational bending with impact parameter, $r$, only the mass $M(r)$ enclosed inside the radius $r$ is relevant.

What should be the mass distribution, $M(r)$, such that the gravitational lens behaves like an ideal optical convex lens?

solution.statement:
**(T10.1)**

Solution:

The rays travelling closer to the gravitational body will bend more. Thus, we get shortest convergence point where the rays just grazing the solar surface will meet each other.

$$\theta_{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}}{R_{\odot}} \simeq \frac{R_{\odot}}{f_{\min}}$$ **[2.0]**

$$\therefore\ f_{\min} = \frac{R_{\odot}^2}{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}} = \frac{R_{\odot}^2 c^2}{4GM_{\odot}}$$ **[2.0]**

$$= \frac{(6.955 \times 10^8 \times 2.998 \times 10^8)^2}{4 \times 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.989 \times 10^{30}}\ \mathrm{m}$$

$$= 8.188 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{m} = \frac{8.188 \times 10^{13}}{1.496 \times 10^{11}}\ \mathrm{AU}$$

$$\boxed{f_{\min} = 547.3\ \mathrm{AU}}$$ **[2.0]**

**(T10.2)**

Solution:

The following figure needs to be drawn. **[1.0]**

The light bending from the surface of the Sun ($r = R_{\odot}$) will intersect the detector at its centre, as it is kept at $f_{\min}$.

The boundary of the detector will be intersected by a light ray with $r = R_{\odot} + h$. This ray will intersect the $x$-axis at a distance $f_2$.

$$f_2 = \frac{(R_{\odot} + h)^2}{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}}$$ **[2.0]**

**Same argument as in Part 1**

For small angles,

$$a = (f_2 - f_{\min})\theta_2$$

$$= \left[\frac{(R_{\odot} + h)^2}{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}} - \frac{R_{\odot}^2}{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}}\right]\frac{2R_{\mathrm{sch}}}{(R_{\odot} + h)} = \frac{2R_{\odot}h + h^2}{R_{\odot} + h}$$ **[2.0]**

$$\simeq 2h$$ **[2.0]**

Let original intensity of the incoming radiation be $I_0$.

The flux at the detector in the presence of Sun is $\Phi_{\odot} = I_0\ 2\pi\ R_{\odot}\ h$ **[1.0]**

The flux at the detector in the absence of Sun is $\Phi_0 = I_0\ \pi\ a^2$ **[1.0]**

The amplification is therefore

$$A_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\Phi_{\odot}}{\Phi_0} = \frac{I_0 2\pi R_{\odot} h}{I_0 \pi a^2} = \boxed{\frac{R_{\odot}}{a}}$$ **[1.0]**

**(T10.3)**

Solution:

All rays should focus at the same spot. This should be evident from figure drawn on answersheet or otherwise. **[2.0]**

Let there be two rays with impact parameters $r_1$ and $r_2$. The corresponding distances of focus will be

$$f_i = \frac{r_i^2}{2r_{\mathrm{sch}_i}} = \frac{r_i^2 c^2}{4GM(r_i)}$$ **[2.0]**

**Same argument as in Part 1**

The rquirement $f_1 = f_2$ implies

$$\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2} = \frac{M(r_1)}{M(r_2)}$$ **[1.0]**

The required mass distribution is: $\boxed{M(r) \propto r^2}$ **[1.0]**

The required mass distribution is: $M(r) \propto r^2$

figures.alt: Ray just grazing the solar limb of radius R_sun, bent by angle θ_b, crossing the x-axis at distance f_min from the Sun's centre.
Two parallel rays with impact parameters R_sun and R_sun + h bent by angle θ_2, intersecting a detector of radius a at distance f_min; f_2 marked to the axis crossing.
Detector figure continued on page 15: rays bent by θ_2 reaching the detector of radius a at f_min, with f_2 marked.
Spherical mass distribution with two rays of impact parameters r_1 and r_2 bent by angles θ_2 and θ_1, both focusing at the same point at distance f_1 = f_2 on the x-axis.

problems.title: Gravitational Waves
problems.statement:
The first signal of gravitational waves was observed by two advanced LIGO detectors at Hanford and Livingston, USA in September 2015. One of these measurements (strain vs time in seconds) is shown in the accompanying figure. In this problem, we will interpret this signal in terms of a small test mass $m$ orbiting around a large mass $M$ (i.e., $m \ll M$), by considering several models for the nature of the central mass.

The test mass loses energy due to the emission of gravitational waves. As a result the orbit keeps on shrinking, until the test mass reaches the surface of the object, or in the case of a black hole, the innermost stable circular orbit – ISCO – which is given by $R_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 3R_{\mathrm{sch}}$, where $R_{\mathrm{sch}}$ is the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. This is the "epoch of merger". At this point, the amplitude of the gravitational wave is maximum, and so is its frequency, which is always twice the orbital frequency. In this problem, we will only focus on the gravitational waves before the merger, when Kepler's laws are assumed to be valid. After the merger, the form of gravitational waves will drastically change.

figures.alt: Графика на GW150914, наблюдаван от LIGO Louisiana: щам $h$ $(\times 10^{21})$ спрямо времето $t$ (s) от 0.275 до около 0.465 s, с нарастваща честота и амплитуда, маркирани „Epoch of Merger“ и „Data Source: LIGO Open Science Centre“.

parts.label: T11.1
parts.statement: Consider the observed gravitational waves shown in the figure above. Estimate the time period, $T_0$, and hence calculate the frequency, $f_0$, of gravitational waves just before the epoch of merger.

parts.label: T11.2
parts.statement:
For any main sequence (MS) star, the radius of the star, $R_{\mathrm{MS}}$, and its mass, $M_{\mathrm{MS}}$, are related by a power law given as,

$$R_{\mathrm{MS}} \propto (M_{\mathrm{MS}})^{\alpha}$$

where $\alpha = 0.8$ for $M_{\odot} < M_{\mathrm{MS}}$ and $\alpha = 1.0$ for $0.08M_{\odot} \leq M_{\mathrm{MS}} \leq M_{\odot}$.

If the central object were a main sequence star, write an expression for the maximum frequency of gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{MS}}$, in terms of mass of the star in units of solar masses ($M_{\mathrm{MS}}/M_{\odot}$) and $\alpha$.

parts.label: T11.3
parts.statement: Using the above result, determine the appropriate value of $\alpha$ that will give the maximum possible frequency of gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{MS,max}}$ for any main sequence star. Evaluate this frequency.

parts.label: T11.4
parts.statement: White dwarf (WD) stars have a maximum mass of $1.44\,M_{\odot}$ (known as the Chandrasekhar limit) and obey the mass-radius relation $R \propto M^{-1/3}$. The radius of a solar mass white dwarf is equal to 6000 km. Find the highest frequency of emitted gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{WD,max}}$, if the test mass is orbiting a white dwarf.

parts.label: T11.5
parts.statement: Neutron stars (NS) are a peculiar type of compact objects which have masses between 1 and $3M_{\odot}$ and radii in the range 10 – 15 km. Find the range of frequencies of emitted gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{NS,min}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{NS,max}}$, if the test mass is orbiting a neutron star at a distance close to the neutron star radius.

parts.label: T11.6
parts.statement: If the test mass is orbiting a black hole (BH), write the expression for the frequency of emitted gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{BH}}$, in terms of mass of the black hole, $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$, and the solar mass $M_{\odot}$.

parts.label: T11.7
parts.statement: Based only on the time period (or frequency) of gravitational waves before the epoch of merger, determine whether the central object can be a main sequence star (MS), a white dwarf (WD), a neutron star (NS), or a black hole (BH). Tick the correct option in the Summary Answersheet. Estimate the mass of this object, $M_{\mathrm{obj}}$, in units of $M_{\odot}$.

solution.statement:
(T11.1)

**Solution:**

From the graph, just before the peak of emission, the time period of gravitational waves is approximately $(0.007 \pm 0.004)\ \mathrm{s}$.

$$T_0 \approx 0.007\ \mathrm{s}$$ **[2.0]**

**Acceptable range:** 0.003 to 0.011 s

That is, the frequency of the gravitational waves is $f_0 \approx 142.86\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **[1.0]**

**Acceptable range:** 333.33 to 90.91 Hz

**Answer given in terms of angular frequency with correct value and units gains full credit.**

(T11.2)

**Solution:**

Since $m \ll M$ then, by Kepler's third law

$$f_{\mathrm{orbital}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r^3}}$$ **[4.0]**

Hence the frequency of the gravitational waves is

$$f_{\mathrm{grav}} = 2f_{\mathrm{orbital}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r^3}}$$ **[1.0]**

The frequency will be maximum when $r = R_{\mathrm{MS}}$. **[1.0]**

For main sequence stars,

$$\frac{R_{\mathrm{MS}}}{R_{\odot}} = \left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}{M_{\odot}}\right)^{\alpha}$$

$$\therefore\ R_{\mathrm{MS}} = R_{\odot}\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}{M_{\odot}}\right)^{\alpha}$$ **[1.0]**

$$\therefore\ f_{\mathrm{MS}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\mathrm{MS}}}{R_{\odot}^3}}\left(\frac{M_{\odot}}{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}\right)^{3\alpha/2}$$

$$= \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3}}\left(\frac{M_{\odot}}{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}\right)^{(3\alpha-1)/2}$$

$$f_{\mathrm{MS}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3}}\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}{M_{\odot}}\right)^{(1-3\alpha)/2}$$ **[3.0]**

(T11.3)

**Solution:**

For possible values of $\alpha$ given in the question, the exponent $\frac{1-3\alpha}{2}$ is negative. Thus, if $M_{\mathrm{MS}} > M_{\odot}$, the frequency will be smaller. Thus, for highest possible frequency coming from a main sequence star, you should take lowest possible mass i.e. $\alpha = 1.0$ **[4.0]**

$$f_{\mathrm{MS,max}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3}}\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}{M_{\odot}}\right)^{\left(\frac{1-3\times 1}{2}\right)}$$

$$= \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{\odot}^3}} \times \frac{M_{\odot}}{M_{\mathrm{MS}}}$$ **[2.0]**

The frequency of gravitational waves will be given by,

$$f_{\mathrm{MS,max}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.989 \times 10^{30}}{(6.955 \times 10^8)^3}} \times \frac{1}{0.08}$$

$$f_{\mathrm{MS,max}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{mHz}$$ **[3.0]**

**Answer given in terms of angular frequency with correct value and units gains full credit.**

(T11.4)

**Solution:**

The maximum frequency would be when $r = R_{\mathrm{WD}}$. **[1.0]**

We use the notation $R_{WD_{\odot}}$ for the radius of a solar mass white dwarf. Then for white dwarfs

$$R_{WD}^3 = R_{WD_{\odot}}^3\,\frac{M_{WD}}{M_{\odot}}$$ **[1.0]**

$$f_{\mathrm{WD}} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\mathrm{WD}}}{R_{WD}^3}}$$

$$= \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{R_{WD_{\odot}}^3}\,\frac{M_{WD}}{M_{\odot}}}$$ **[2.0]**

For maximum frequency, we have to take highest white dwarf mass. **[2.0]**

$$f_{\mathrm{WD,max}} = 2.600 \times 10^{-6} \times \sqrt{\frac{1.989 \times 10^{30}}{(6000 \times 10^3)^3}} \times 1.44$$

problems.title: AstroSat
problems.statement:
India astronomy satellite, AstroSat, launched in September 2015, has five different instruments.

In this question, we will discuss three of these instruments (SXT, LAXPC, CZTI), which point in the same direction and observe in X-ray wavelengths. The details of these instruments are given in the table below.

| Instrument | Band [keV] | Collecting Area [m$^2$] | Effective Photon Detection Efficiency | Saturation level [counts] | No. of Pixels |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SXT | 0.3 – 80 | 0.067 | 60% | 15000 (total) | 512 x 512 |
| LAXPC | 3 – 80 | 1.5 | 40% | 50000 (in any one counter) or 200000 (total) | --- |
| CZTI | 10 – 150 | 0.09 | 50% | --- | 4 x 4096 |

You should note that LAXPC energy range is divided into 8 different energy band counters of equal bandwidth with no overlap.

These instruments were used to observe an X-ray source (assumed to be a point source), whose energy spectrum followed the power law,

$$F(E) = KE^{-2/3} \qquad \left[\text{in units of counts/keV/m}^2/\text{s}\right]$$

where $E$ is the energy in keV, $K$ is a constant and $F(E)$ is photon flux density at that energy. Photon flux density, by definition, is given for per unit collecting area (m$^2$) per unit bandwidth (keV) and per unit time (seconds). From prior observations, we know that the source has a flux density of 10 counts/keV/m$^2$/s at 1 keV, when measured by a detector with 100% photon detection efficiency. The "counts" here mean the number of photons reported by the detector.

As the source flux follows the power law given above, we know that for a given energy range from $E_1$ (lower energy) to $E_2$ (higher energy) the total photon flux ($F_{\mathrm{T}}$) will be given by

$$F_{\mathrm{T}} = 3K\left(E_2^{1/3} - E_1^{1/3}\right) \qquad \left[\text{in units of counts/m}^2/\text{s}\right]$$

From parts (T12.1) and (T12.9)

$$v_{\mathrm{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM_{\odot}}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.989 \times 10^{30}}{3.97 \times 10^{10}}} = 57.798\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$$ **[1.0]**

Assumption of small planet ($M_{\mathrm{p}} \ll M_{\mathrm{s}}$) is valid because $\Delta$ is very small; less dense planet would make the assumption stronger!

$$M_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{s}}v_0}{v_{\mathrm{p}}} = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{30} \times 0.400}{5.7798 \times 10^{4} \times 5.972 \times 10^{24}} M_{\oplus} = \boxed{2.30\ M_{\oplus}}$$ **[2.0]**

From part (T12.4),

$$R_{\mathrm{p}} = R_{\mathrm{s}}\sqrt{\Delta}$$

From part (T12.7),

$$\frac{a}{R_{\mathrm{s}}} = \frac{2P\Delta^{1/4}}{\pi(t_{\mathrm{T}}^{2} - t_{\mathrm{F}}^{2})^{1/2}} = \frac{2P\Delta^{1/4}}{\pi t_{\mathrm{T}}(1 - (t_{\mathrm{F}}/t_{\mathrm{T}})^{2})^{1/2}}$$

$$\therefore\ R_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{a\pi t_{\mathrm{T}}(1 - (t_{\mathrm{F}}/t_{\mathrm{T}})^{2})^{1/2}}{2P\Delta^{1/4}}$$

Combining,

$$R_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{a\pi t_{\mathrm{T}}(1 - (t_{\mathrm{F}}/t_{\mathrm{T}})^{2})^{1/2}\Delta^{1/2}}{2P\Delta^{1/4}}$$

$$= \frac{a\pi t_{\mathrm{T}}(1 - (t_{\mathrm{F}}/t_{\mathrm{T}})^{2})^{1/2}\Delta^{1/4}}{2P}$$ **[2.0]**

$$= \frac{3.97 \times 10^{10} \times \pi \times \frac{1}{24} \times (1 - 0.8519^{2})^{1/2} \times (0.0064)^{1/4}}{2 \times 50.0 \times 6.371 \times 10^{6}} R_{\oplus}$$

$$= \boxed{1.21\ R_{\oplus}}$$ **[1.0]**

Mean density

$$\rho_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{p}}}{4\pi R_{\mathrm{p}}^{3}/3} = \frac{2.30}{(1.21)^{3}} \rho_{\oplus} = 1.3\rho_{\oplus}$$ **[1.0]**

Since mean density is higher than that of Earth, the planet is $\boxed{\mathrm{Rocky}}$. **[1.0]**
